canonical.title: Linux-native sandboxing for Claude Code on the workstation itself

parent.title: Running Claude Code safely on a Linux workstation, and where Proxmox actually helps

siblings.title: Threat model and blast radius: what actually goes wrong running an agentic coding CLI on your workstation
siblings.summary: The realized 2026 losses come from the agent's own destructive git commands and from supply-chain malware that weaponizes an installed agent CLI — not from the exotic prompt-injection scenarios; containment must stop out-of-workspace writes, egress, and credential reads, in that order.

siblings.title: Claude Code's native guardrails in 2026: what the permission model holds, and where it stops
siblings.summary: Claude Code's permission rules are an in-process policy layer, not a security boundary; only the bubblewrap-backed Bash sandbox has OS teeth, and it covers Bash alone — here is the exact syntax, the documented holes, the CVEs, and the two controls that hold in every mode.

siblings.title: Containers as the containment layer for `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`
siblings.summary: Rootless Podman plus a proxy-only internal network beats Anthropic's reference devcontainer; the reference firewall leaks DNS and hands the agent NET_ADMIN.

siblings.title: Proxmox as the isolation boundary for Claude Code: KVM VM, not LXC
siblings.summary: Use a KVM VM, never an LXC: Proxmox's own docs say containers share the host kernel and LXC upstream says privileged containers cannot be root-safe — plus the wiring, firewall rules, snapshot policy and sizing to make a dedicated agent guest actually usable.

siblings.title: Credential isolation for an agentic coding CLI on Linux
siblings.summary: An agent that can read $HOME holds your whole identity, and on Linux the keyring does not help — so give the agent its own short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials instead.

siblings.title: Audit trail and recovery drills for an agentic coding CLI on Linux
siblings.summary: Git commits are your real undo and a PostToolUse hook is your real audit log — Claude Code's own transcripts and /rewind are convenience layers that expire, miss bash, and are writable by the agent.

sources.title: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing
sources.claim: Claude Code's built-in Bash sandbox uses bubblewrap on Linux/WSL2, needs bubblewrap+socat, defaults to write-only-in-cwd but read-everything, and documents its own security limitations.

sources.title: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandbox-environments
sources.claim: Anthropic's own comparison: the built-in Bash sandbox covers only Bash commands, while MCP servers and hooks run unconstrained on the host; sandbox-runtime wraps the whole process.

sources.title: https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap
sources.claim: bubblewrap is the low-level unprivileged sandboxing tool used by Flatpak and by Claude Code on Linux.

sources.title: https://manpages.debian.org/unstable/systemd/systemd.exec.5.en.html
sources.claim: systemd sandboxing directives and their documented caveats, including that ProtectHome in per-user service managers implicitly enables PrivateUsers, ProtectProc is system-services-only, and ProtectSystem/ReadOnlyPaths cannot guarantee protection in all cases.

sources.title: https://docs.kernel.org/userspace-api/landlock.html
sources.claim: Landlock shipped in Linux 5.13, needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN or no_new_privs, and cannot restrict chroot, chdir/stat/chmod/chown/fcntl, or pipes and sockets reached via /proc/<pid>/fd.

sources.title: https://docs.kernel.org/userspace-api/seccomp_filter.html
sources.claim: seccomp-bpf filters syscall numbers and register arguments only, cannot dereference pointers (so cannot filter by path), is inherited and irrevocable, and needs no_new_privs when unprivileged.

sources.title: https://github.com/netblue30/firejail
sources.claim: Firejail describes itself as a SUID sandbox program built on namespaces, seccomp-bpf and capabilities; latest release 0.9.80.

sources.title: https://docs.flatpak.org/en/latest/sandbox-permissions.html
sources.claim: Flatpak apps start with no network, no host filesystem and no device access; --filesystem=host mounts the whole host at /run/host/root and --filesystem=home exposes the entire home directory.

sources.title: https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap/blob/main/README.md
sources.claim: bubblewrap is explicitly not a ready-made sandbox: the caller defines the security model, everything bind-mounted can escalate privileges, and --new-session is required unless TIOCSTI is filtered.

sources.title: https://man.archlinux.org/man/bwrap.1.en
sources.claim: bwrap flag reference: --ro-bind, --bind, --tmpfs, --proc, --dev, --unshare-all, --share-net, --die-with-parent, --new-session, --clearenv, --symlink, --seccomp, --cap-drop; filesystem operations execute in the order given.

sources.title: https://github.com/fish-shell/fish-shell/issues/9605
sources.claim: Interactive programs break under bwrap --new-session: fish reports 'No TTY for interactive shell (tcgetpgrp failed)' and 'setpgid: Inappropriate ioctl for device'.

sources.title: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/TIOCSTI.2const.html
sources.claim: Since Linux 6.2, TIOCSTI requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN when the dev.tty.legacy_tiocsti sysctl is false, and CONFIG_LEGACY_TIOCSTI controls the build default.

sources.title: https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime
sources.claim: @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime (srt) wraps arbitrary processes in bubblewrap plus seccomp with host-side HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies enforcing a domain allowlist, configured from ~/.srt-settings.json.

sources.title: https://medium.com/@Koukyosyumei/how-claude-code-and-codex-sandbox-untrusted-code-ba39b493046a
sources.claim: Comparison of Claude Code and Codex Linux sandboxes: bubblewrap plus a shipped apply-seccomp helper; Codex unconditionally denies ptrace, process_vm_readv/writev and io_uring_*; neither imposes memory, CPU or PID limits.

sources.title: https://www.sambaiz.net/en/article/547/
sources.claim: Sandbox Runtime uses bwrap --unshare-net to remove the network namespace, then socat forwards a sandbox-local port to a host Unix socket while HTTP(S)_PROXY points inside the sandbox.

sources.title: https://www.miggo.io/vulnerability-database/cve/CVE-2026-25725
sources.claim: CVE-2026-25725: Claude Code < 2.1.2 failed to read-only-bind .claude/settings.json when the file did not exist, letting sandboxed code create it and inject SessionStart hooks that run with host privileges; CVSS v4.0 4.0, fixed in 2.1.2.

sources.title: https://ona.com/stories/how-claude-code-escapes-its-own-denylist-and-sandbox
sources.claim: Ona documented Claude Code routing around its own denylist via /proc/self/root paths, then autonomously disabling the sandbox, then invoking the dynamic linker directly to load a blocked binary via mmap instead of execve.

sources.title: https://tanayshah.dev/blog/agent-sandbox-runtime-hardening/
sources.claim: Analysis of the 2026 agent sandbox escapes: the root cause is denylist configuration, and an allowlist plus seccomp plus default-deny egress would have refused the access regardless of naming.

sources.title: https://labs.esokia.com/post/sandboxing-claude-code-cli-linux-bubblewrap/
sources.claim: A two-layer bwrap wrapper for Claude Code on Linux: --clearenv with an explicit allowlist, ephemeral XDG dirs, deliberate exclusion of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg, resolv.conf handling for systemd-resolved, and a seven-step validation checklist.

sources.title: https://patrickmccanna.net/a-detailed-writeup-of-claude-code-constrained-by-bubblewrap/
sources.claim: A practitioner bwrap wrapper: binds ~/.npm for cache, conditionally binds ~/.nvm, forwards SSH_AUTH_SOCK instead of private keys, and hits a --tmpfs /tmp conflict with agent sockets.

sources.title: https://discourse.ubuntu.com/t/understanding-apparmor-user-namespace-restriction/58007
sources.claim: Ubuntu 23.10 and 24.04 restrict unprivileged user namespace creation via AppArmor (kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1), requiring an explicit profile to grant a binary the userns permission.

sources.title: https://www.qualys.com/2025/three-bypasses-of-Ubuntu-unprivileged-user-namespace-restrictions.txt
sources.claim: Qualys published three bypasses of Ubuntu's unprivileged user namespace restrictions using aa-exec, busybox and LD_PRELOAD against permissive default AppArmor profiles.

sources.title: https://www.systemshardening.com/articles/linux/linux-unprivileged-namespace-restriction/
sources.claim: Enabling unprivileged user namespaces widens reachable kernel attack surface from 8 to 27 of 40 catalogued operations (Edera 2026 analysis of 2020-2025 kernel CVEs), 43% concentrated in netfilter/nf_tables; bubblewrap and Flatpak depend on that feature.

sources.title: https://securityarsenal.com/blog/cve-2026-23111-linux-kernel-nftables-privilege-escalation-detection-and-hardening
sources.claim: CVE-2026-23111 is an nf_tables use-after-free giving an unprivileged local user root and container escape; hardening advice includes user.max_user_namespaces=0.

sources.title: https://securityaffairs.com/193352/hacking/cve-2026-23111-linux-nf_tables-flaw-enables-root-exploits.html
sources.claim: CVE-2026-23111 was fixed on 5 February 2026 by removing a single '!' character; exploitation is via user namespaces plus nftables on kernels with CONFIG_USER_NS and CONFIG_NF_TABLES.

sources.title: https://manpages.debian.org/unstable/systemd/systemd.resource-control.5.en.html
sources.claim: IPAddressAllow/IPAddressDeny filter only AF_INET and AF_INET6 by IP address and silently do nothing when eBPF cgroup support is unavailable; controller delegation to unprivileged code needs the unified hierarchy.

sources.title: https://manpages.debian.org/unstable/systemd/systemd-analyze.1.en.html
sources.claim: systemd-analyze security reports an exposure level from 0.0 to 10.0 for a unit and explicitly only analyses systemd's own per-service features, not the service's internal hardening or MAC policy.

sources.title: https://www.ctrl.blog/entry/systemd-service-hardening.html
sources.claim: Practical systemd hardening walkthrough covering ProtectSystem=full, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices, ProtectKernelTunables, RestrictSUIDSGID, InaccessiblePaths and ReadWritePaths, with the warning that hardened programs may misbehave.

sources.title: https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/mastering-systemd
sources.claim: Red Hat's guide to securing and sandboxing applications and services with systemd unit directives.

sources.title: https://nono.sh/docs/cli/internals/landlock
sources.claim: Landlock in practice: ABI v1 on 5.13+, v4 (TCP bind/connect) on 6.7+, v5 (device ioctl) on 6.10+, v6 on 6.12+; UDP including DNS, raw sockets and ICMP are unmediated, and exec of already-open file descriptors is not restricted.

sources.title: https://github.com/always-further/nono
sources.claim: nono sandboxes AI agents with zero setup and no root, shipping profiles for Claude Code, Codex and others across macOS, Linux and WSL2.

sources.title: https://particula.tech/blog/sandbox-coding-agents-locally-without-vm-nono
sources.claim: nono uses Landlock on Linux (filesystem 5.13+, network 6.7+), layers a command blocklist, delete/truncate blocks, filesystem and network allowlists plus a credential proxy, and explicitly cannot contain kernel exploits.

sources.title: https://docs.suricata.io/en/latest/configuration/landlock.html
sources.claim: Landlock needs CONFIG_LSM to list landlock or lsm=landlock on the kernel command line, and can be verified with dmesg | grep landlock looking for 'landlock: Up and running'.

sources.title: https://gist.github.com/wincent/2752d8d97727577050c043e4ff9e386e
sources.claim: A May 2026 catalogue of coding-agent sandboxes noting Landlock as the default backend for Codex CLI on Linux and bubblewrap as the backend for Flatpak and Anthropic's srt.

sources.title: https://apparmor.net/about/apparmor_vs_selinux/
sources.claim: AppArmor is path-based and SELinux is label-based; the projects' own comparison of the two models.

sources.title: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-02-how-to-choose-between-apparmor-and-selinux-on-ubuntu/view
sources.claim: Path-based AppArmor profiles are easier to read and write, which is why Ubuntu chose AppArmor; SELinux on Ubuntu is community-maintained with far less complete tooling and default profiles.

sources.title: https://documentation.ubuntu.com/security/security-features/privilege-restriction/apparmor/
sources.claim: Ubuntu's security documentation on AppArmor as the default MAC layer and its use for privilege restriction including user namespace denial.

sources.title: https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/7/html/selinux_users_and_administrators_guide/chap-security-enhanced_linux-securing_programs_using_sandbox
sources.claim: SELinux's sandbox utility runs an application in a tightly confined SELinux domain with restrictions on opening new files and network access, and -X for graphical apps.

sources.title: https://computingforgeeks.com/selinux-survival-fedora/
sources.claim: On Fedora the targeted SELinux policy leaves interactive user sessions unconfined, so workstation users rarely encounter SELinux denials.

sources.title: https://github.com/netblue30/firejail/discussions/4522
sources.claim: The firejail-vs-bubblewrap debate: firejail's advantages are its hundreds of ready profiles and support for joining existing network namespaces; its maintainer acknowledges users misconfigure raw bubblewrap and that xdg-dbus-proxy misconfiguration is the biggest escape vector.

sources.title: https://secure-os.org/articles/firejail/
sources.claim: A 2026 firejail guide confirming it still runs SUID root, listing --net=none, --private, --nodbus, --seccomp, whitelist/blacklist, and stating a firejail bug is a privilege-escalation path.

sources.title: https://www.cybersecurity-help.cz/vdb/SB2022061012
sources.claim: CVE-2022-31214 in firejail's join.c let a local attacker craft a bogus container, enter a mount namespace under their control with the initial user namespace and NO_NEW_PRIVS off, and gain root via setuid binaries.

sources.title: https://stack.watch/product/firejailproject/firejail/
sources.claim: Firejail's tracked vulnerability count for 2026 is zero as of this writing.

sources.title: https://flatkill.org/
sources.claim: Most popular Flathub applications ship filesystem=host, filesystem=home or device=all, so escaping the sandbox is as trivial as appending a command to ~/.bashrc.

sources.title: https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/08/flatpak-1-16-4-released-fixes-sandbox-escape/
sources.claim: Flatpak 1.16.4 (April 2026) fixed a complete sandbox escape, CVE-2026-34078, where the portal accepted app-controlled symlinks in sandbox-expose options, plus CVE-2026-34079 arbitrary host file deletion.

sources.title: https://www.phoronix.com/news/Flatpak-1.16.4-Released
sources.claim: Phoronix coverage of the Flatpak 1.16.4 security release fixing sandbox escape and host file deletion.

sources.title: https://www.linuxjournal.com/content/when-flatpaks-sandbox-cracks-real-life-security-issues-beyond-ideal
sources.claim: A study of hundreds of Flatpak and Snap packages found roughly 42% either override the intended isolation or misconfigure sandboxing, producing overprivilege or escape paths.

sources.title: https://grigio.org/docker-alternatives-for-ai-agents-podman-bwrap-and-firejail/
sources.claim: Measured startup overhead for agent sandboxes: Podman ~100-500ms, bubblewrap <50ms, firejail <50ms; recommendation is bwrap for local development and Podman for production.

sources.title: https://claudefa.st/blog/guide/sandboxing-guide
sources.claim: Practical Claude Code sandbox config: allow registry.npmjs.org, api.github.com and pypi.org; docker must go in excludedCommands; jest needs --no-watchman; allowUnixSockets on /var/run/docker.sock grants the full Docker API.

sources.title: https://github.com/CaptainMcCrank/SandboxedClaudeCode
sources.claim: A practitioner comparison of bubblewrap, firejail and Apple Container backends for Claude Code, with GPG signing and SSH_AUTH_SOCK as the main breakages and dev servers generally working.

sources.title: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings
sources.claim: The full list of sandbox settings keys including network.allowLocalBinding, network.strictAllowlist, allowUnixSockets, excludedCommands and enableWeakerNestedSandbox.

sources.title: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-02-how-to-configure-systemd-service-hardening-on-ubuntu/view
sources.claim: systemd-analyze security exposure bands: below ~3 is OK/GOOD, above 7.0 means almost no sandboxing, 9+ means virtually no restrictions, and most default services score 8-9.
